7 Workflows with dry-run publishing Where this number comes from

The problem

Social content is a treadmill. Someone has to think of the idea, write it in two languages, check it is on-brand, schedule it, and then remember to look at what happened. Most of that is judgement-shaped rather than mechanical, which is exactly why it never gets automated and exactly why it eats a week.

What it does

01

Writes from a brand strategy

Not generic captions. The generator works from a written brand position, in English and Egyptian Arabic, so the output sounds like the account it is posting to.

02

Grades itself before a human sees it

A second model from a different lab scores each draft against the brief and sends it back if it fails, with lint gates behind it. Two models from two labs rarely make the same mistake.

03

Stops at a human

Nothing publishes without an approval. The gate is the point: the agent does the work, the person keeps the judgement call.

04

Studies a simulated result

Synthetic engagement feeds the analyst and illustrates how the next brief could use feedback.

How it is built

BriefDraftJudgeHuman gateDry runReview

A generator and a judge use different models inside deterministic n8n workflows. The test path records publishing payloads for review. The feedback pass uses simulated engagement.

What I'd watch if it were yours

A judge is cheaper than a rewrite

The scoring pass costs a fraction of generation and kills most of the bad output before a person spends attention on it.

Cross-lab, not cross-prompt

Asking the same model to review itself catches far less. The value comes from a genuinely different model.

The gate is a feature to sell, not a limitation to hide

Buyers are afraid of AI publishing something embarrassing under their name. An approval step answers that objection better than any accuracy claim.

Tested with dry-run publishing for 8 batches and 56 posts. The code and evidence are public at github.com/Moamen-Elsharkawy/instabay-agent.
